author: Bausee
quote:
I was looking forward to this game for YEARS. Unfortunately, it’s exceptionally disappointing. 

A slow burn Bonnie and Clyde story that dials back the fun for the sake of realism is just not what I, and many other players, want. 

The characters are wildly unlikable, Jason for being an emotionless, monotone moron, and Lucia for being a ****. Trevor was a massive ****, but he was LIKEABLE. Lucia is an ****, but she’s not even remotely likable. 

The gunplay feels off, the movement is delayed and sluggish, the forced romantic aspect is arduous at best, optimization is awful. Rockstar’s ambitions were bigger than their talent. This game needed another few months to cook, it is not ready. 

It’s not all bad though. It is pretty to look at when the frame rate isn’t plummeting.

author: Bausee
quote:
The game is beautiful to look at, and the sights held my attention for a little bit. But once the sense of wonder wore off, I found myself rather underwhelmed. The gameplay loop is monotonous, and feels very similar to Black Desert Online: grind in order to take on this tough boss so you can continue grinding to take on the next tough boss, to grind some more. It didn’t feel like I was working toward anything meaningful. The side quests you have to grind out are often boring, soulless, and completely unrelated to anything. A lot of MMO style fetch quests, which was really disappointing. The controls are really uncomfortable, and the lack of an option to change them at all is mind boggling. I lost tons progress to bugs 3 times. And the combat was… just okay.  

Overall, I think that they didn’t learn from the boring gameplay loop of BDO and just implemented it again. This is probably because it was supposed to be an MMO prequel to BDO, but they had plenty of time to give us something fresh and exciting, and they didn’t. They promised so much and unfortunately it fell short on almost every one. 

Many players expected this to be the new touchstone in gaming. Unfortunately it failed to live up to the hype. Hopefully it will receive some post launch patches to fix a lot of the glaring issues.

author: Bausee
quote:
I want to start off by saying -I enjoyed the game-. Is it amazing? No. Is it horrible? No. It’s a good game, it’s just a really bad Dragon Age game. 

The story has a great premise, but it’s really poorly executed. BioWare games are known for making tough decisions with longstanding consequences that carry over from game to game. Decisions in previous games do not affect Veilguard, except for 3 minor decisions from Inquisiton dlc which you choose in the character creator. Disappointing, but I got over it. What I did find worse is that the decisions you make in the course of Veilguard are very few, and the seldom decision you do make is entirely inconsequential. The game plays out nearly identically no matter how you play. 

Companions are fairly dull, too. With the exception of Neve Gallus, who was an established character prior to this game, they’re all forgettable and lacked nuance. Even Harding, who was a minor character from Inquisiton turned full companion in Veilguard, was uninteresting. Taash, who comes out as non-binary in the course of their story, is a glaring problem with the character writing. While I love seeing different forms of life experience represented in gaming, this character’s story arc was so poorly executed it was difficult to play through. Supposedly a fierce dragon hunter, this character comes out as non-binary, and that’s where the depth ends. Their entire story is about them coming out, it’s not used as a way to build the character, it’s not an aspect of the character, this is the entire character. As a member of the LGBT community, I found it so hamfisted, preachy, and pandering. Most of the companions are written to express themselves like edgy 14 year olds and the player character is constantly talking to them as if they’re children, overexplaining everything.

RPG mechanics are extremely shallow, and combat, while fun at first, is extremely boring. The lack of enemy variety, and the limited amount of skills at your disposal (3) make for a very dull combat experience. Combat also does not fit within the lore of the series, where being a mage was a very consequential thing, in Veilguard all classes and companions are essentially mages as everyone has magical abilities. 

The world design is awful. The scenery is beautiful, but the areas you’re able to run around in are mostly just hallways decorated to look like worlds. Nothing feels cohesive, even the cities aren’t believable. Running around Minrathous doesn’t feel like being in a city, it doesn’t feel lived in, it feels like what it is: a series of interconnected hallways. 

The character design leaves a lot to be desired as well. The new, stylized direction they went with doesn’t lend itself very well to the story they’re trying to tell. What was once a story that felt dark and menacing has become quirky, light-hearted, and reminiscent of a children’s fairytale. The final moments of the game are very much trying to go for the same feeling as the Suicide Mission from Mass Effect 2, but there isn’t a single ounce of tension in this game. Because everything we do and the decisions that we make leading up to that moment don’t matter, neither does what you decide to do in the final mission. One of your companions is going to die, and the only consequential decision you make is who it’s going to be. 

While the new stylized approach is something that can be more or less overlooked as you become accustomed to it, the enemy design is atrocious. What were once frightening and grotesque monsters are now little more than cartoonish Halloween decorations - this is not an exaggeration. 

Character creation is fairly robust, but there are a number of really questionable choices when it comes to what was included, and what was not. Representation is important and something I advocate for, but it’s strange that vitiligo, which represents very few players, is present, but something like body hair, which 99.99% of players naturally have, is not. Body proportions are also very limited, It’s a wonder why they added certain sliders at all.

I think that the worst part of the game, however, is that you cannot be who you want to be. You are not playing as a character of your choosing, you’re playing as Rook, who cannot be anyone other than an overly compassionate, good natured person. There are no ruthless or morally questionable choices you can make. Unlike in other dragon age games where your choices mattered to your team, and they might leave and never come back if you made egregious decisions, it’s impossible to piss off your companions in Veilguard. The game offers absolutely no player agency.

If you want to play this game, it’s worth a playthrough, but get it on a heavily discounted sale. Again, as a game it’s just okay. But as a dragon age game, it’s awful.
